profile.summary: Zacharias speaks to a small Jewish community, tired and pressured after Babylonian exile, when the temple was still in reconstruction and national life seemed fragile. In the midst of external opposition, internal discouragement and moral and social flaws, the prophet calls the people to repentance, spiritual renewal and practical obedience to the covenant. His visions link the present of Jerusalem to the future of God: the Lord remains committed to his people, will return to dwell among him and extend his rule over the whole earth. The book combines exhortation, comfort and Messianic hope, insisting that true worship and community restoration go together with justice, mercy and fidelity.
profile.setting: The context is the post-exallic period, after Cyrus' decree in 538 BC, when Jews returned from Babylon to Judah and Jerusalem. The founding of a new temple had been launched, but the project was interrupted for nearly two decades, under political pressure, economic difficulties and spiritual aridity. Zechariah ministers in Jerusalem along with Haggai, beginning in 520 BC, to encourage the people to resume the work and, at the same time, to promote moral and spiritual renewal. The first part of the book fits well in this immediate setting; the final chapters, without explicit date, project hope beyond the rebuilding of the temple, emphasizing future restoration, judgment on the nations and the full manifestation of the kingdom of God. The authorship is traditionally attributed to Zacharias, the son of Berechiah and grandson of Ido, but the date and composition of the final sections are discussed by some scholars; yet, there is still a strong indication of literary unity throughout the book.

structure.label: Called to Repentance and Early Visions
structure.description: Exhortation to the return to the Lord, followed by visions that communicate comfort, warning, and the sovereign action of God in behalf of Jerusalem and the leadership of his people.

structure.label: Fasting, justice and community restoration
structure.description: Correction of empty religiosity and reaffirmation that the proper response to the covenant involves justice, mercy, fidelity and hope in the restoration of Zion.

structure.label: Future hope and government of God
structure.description: Oracles of judgment and hope that proclaim the intervention of the Lord, the protection of his people and the prospect of a just king linked to peace and salvation.

structure.label: Final Deliverment and Lord's Kingdom
structure.description: Vision of the final conflict, purification of the people and establishment of the universal government of God, culminating in the holiness of Jerusalem.

themes: Repentance and return to the Lord
Restoration of Jerusalem and the temple
Social justice as a fruit of fidelity to the covenant
Messianic hope and future government of God
Comfort of the slaughtered and warning to the infidels
readingKeys: Notice how visions and oracles link the people's difficult present to the future hope given by God.
Note the strong connection between temple worship and ethical practice: restoration is not only architectural, but spiritual and social.
Notice the questions about fasting, the criticism of empty religiosity and insistence on justice, mercy and fidelity in daily life.
profile.cautions: Some compositional questions remain debated, especially the precise date of the final sections and the hypothesis of different authors; however, the introduction supports a reading of the book's literary unit. For the evangelical reader, it is important not to separate future hope from present obedience: Zechariah unites Messianic promise, just community life and renewal of the people of God.

dossier.narratedEra: The post-exile Persian period, when Judah/Jerusalem had already returned from exile and the restored community lived under pressure from neighboring peoples; visions and sermões also project a Messianic and eschatological future in which Jerusalem will be restored and the Lord will reign over the whole earth.
dossier.compositionEra: The main setting is 520-518 BC, in the reign of Darius, with the ministry of Zechariah beginning two months after that of Haggai and following for at least two years. The first section of the book (caps. 1-8) is located between 520 and 515 BC; the messages without date (caps. 9-14) may have been composed later, perhaps up to 500-470 BC. The source also mentions the academic hypothesis of a division in "Second Zacharias" (9-11) and "Third Zechariah" (12-14), but observes literary continuity and support for unified composition.

politics.title: Persian dominion and the reign of Darius
politics.detail: The historical frame is the Persian empire, with Darius reigning in 521-486 BC; Zechariah prophesied in the early years of this period and the dates of the sermons are anchored in it.
politics.readingImpact: The book is not born in a devotional vacuum, but in a concrete imperial setting: the restoration of Jerusalem happens under foreign sovereignty, which explains the tension between theological hope and political fragility.

politics.title: Return Authorized by Cyrus and Zorobabel Government
politics.detail: Cyrus authorized the return of deportees in 538 BC; the first repatriates were led by Sesbazar, and the restored community had Zorobabel as governor mentioned in the prophetic notes and speeches.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that the restoration announced by Zacharias begins with concrete civil leadership, not only with abstract hope; the message dialogues with a people already installed on earth, but still politically vulnerable.

politics.title: Opposition of neighboring nations
politics.detail: The notes say that the returned ones were oppressed, hostiled and harassed by neighboring nations, which left them discouraged and with the temple in ruins; the first vision also announces judgment against the nations that overthrew Jerusalem and scattered Judah.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of visions becomes of consolation and political reversal: God sees the regional conflict and promises to intervene against the oppressors, so that the restoration of worship also depends on divine protection.

politics.title: Internal disputes on Community practices
politics.detail: In 7:1-14, Bethel delegates ask about fasting; Zechariah answers with rhetorical questions about their motivation and counters empty religious practices to the social justice demanded by God.
politics.readingImpact: The political-moral focus is not only on external enemies, but in the life of the restored community itself: worship, authority and public conduct need to be reorganized before the full blessing.

customs.title: Jejuns linked to national disasters
customs.detail: The notes mention a summer fast that lamented the destruction of Solomon's temple and another in the early autumn that could recall the murder of Gedaliah or even the Day of Atonement.
customs.readingImpact: Chapter 7 makes it clear that community mourning practices were alive in the post-exile; Zacharias shifts the rite issue itself to the spiritual and ethical purpose of the people.

customs.title: Sacrifice and religious consultation as a social gesture
customs.detail: The Bethel delegation seems to have sought for the Lord with some offering or sacrifice, which shows a formal and public religious consultation.
customs.readingImpact: The scene helps the reader to see that the question about fasting is not merely private; it involves cultual procedure and community discernment before the temple in reconstruction.

customs.title: Legal protection of vulnerable
customs.detail: The notes claim that widows, orphans, foreigners and poor often did not have access to common legal protection, and therefore Zechariah includes them in the demands of justice and mercy.
customs.readingImpact: Post-exile religion is read as inseparable from social care: the community can only expect divine favor if it treats the vulnerable.

customs.title: Feast of Tabernacles as memory and hope
customs.detail: In 14:16, the Feast of Tabernacles is described as the beginning of the autumn harvest and memorial of experience in the desert after the exodus; it also functioned as a time of gratitude and social care.
customs.readingImpact: The future worship of the nations in Jerusalem is read in the light of a concrete historical feast; this gives chapter 14 a dimension of worship, provision and pilgrimage, not just political triumph.

customs.title: Household objects and temple utensils
customs.detail: The notes speak of kitchen pots and bells of the king as common items that, in the future kingdom, will become "Holy to the Lord."
customs.readingImpact: Holiness will not be restricted to the sanctuary: even daily life and the most banal objects will be reconfigured by the divine presence.

language.title: The Lord of Armies as a language of encouragement
language.detail: In 1:3, the title is explained as a reference to God's power over an immense angelic army; the note highlights that the expression intends to encourage the Jews.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that restoration is sustained by heavenly authority, not by limited human resources.

language.title: Night views with angelic mediator
language.detail: The introduction of the views follows a pattern: description, request for explanation and interpretation by an angelic messenger. The angel of vision is identified with the Angel of the Lord.
language.readingImpact: The book should be read as visionary prophecy, in which symbols need interpretation; this avoids simplistic literalistic reading of each image.

language.title: Images of horns and craftsmen
language.detail: The horns symbolize power and authority, and may represent rulers, dynasties or nations; the artisans can be widely understood as masters of office able to overthrow these powers.
language.readingImpact: Language transforms international conflict into a plastic image of power crushed by divine action, reinforcing that the empire is not absolute.

language.title: Holistic of holiness: from temple to kitchen
language.detail: The note on 14:20-21 states that the holiness of the Messianic kingdom will reach ordinary utensils, dissolving the distinction between sacred and profane.
language.readingImpact: The final view not only deals with liturgy, but of a whole social order reconsecrated; daily life becomes a sphere of devotion.

timeline.title: 538 BC: decree of Cyrus for return
timeline.detail: Cyrus allowed peoples deported by the Babylonians to return to their ancestral lands.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone explains why the community of Zechariah is already in Jerusalem, but still without full stability; the prophecy is born within the incomplete process of restoration.

timeline.title: 538-536 BC: the foundation of the second temple and later abandonment
timeline.detail: Under the initial administration of the return, the repatriates laid the foundations of a new temple, but the project was later abandoned for nearly two decades.
timeline.readingImpact: The book responds to a prolonged crisis of discouragement: Zechariah speaks of an interrupted work, not to a community already consolidated.

timeline.title: 520 BC: beginning of the ministry of Zechariah
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Zechariah began to prophesy two months after Haggai; the eight visions and the first sermões are located in this period.
timeline.readingImpact: This date guides the reading of 1-6 as a word for a specific moment of resumption of community worship and reconstruction.

timeline.title: 518 BC: Last message dated
timeline.detail: The source reports that the last dated message of Zechariah occurred in 518 BC, while chapters 7-8 come about two years after the visions.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps to see a real progression in the prophetic ministry: initial visions, then pastoral instructions and, finally, questions about fasting and justice practices.

timeline.title: 515 BC: Temple conclusion
timeline.detail: The temple was completed in March 515 BC, under Darius I, although Zechariah 1-8 made no explicit reference to the completed dedication.
timeline.readingImpact: The absence of this reference is relevant to date the first half of the book and to note that the main objective was still to motivate spiritual restoration, not to celebrate the final result.

timeline.title: Future not dated in caps. 9 to 14
timeline.detail: The final messages are presented with no date and may have been composed later, perhaps between 500 and 470 BC; the source also admits academic debate on internal divisions, although it holds literary unity.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader must distinguish Jerusalem from the immediate post-exile of Jerusalem of future judgment and restoration; the final chapters broaden the horizon beyond the reconstruction of the temple.

investigation: The secondary source is selective and comments more intensely certain key verses than others; therefore, many social and historical aspects of the book do not appear in the same detail.
The proposals for dating for chapters 9-14 are presented as a possibility, not as certainty, and the source itself records debate on "Second" and "Third Zechariah."
Notes favor theological and pastoral reading; historical references appear above all when they serve to understand the Persian setting, the temple and community ethics.
There is no historical evidence here independent of the ancient facts; it is what the notes affirm or infer from the biblical text and of the mentioned parallels.
Some topics relevant to exegetical study may be underrepresented because the attached notes do not discuss them directly, especially in excerpts without specific comments.
dossier.limits: This dossier was elaborated only with the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, without resorting to external information. Therefore, the coverage is necessarily partial and follows the cutout of the comments provided. Where the source speaks clearly, the item was marked as explicit-source; where the connection depends on inference from the grade, used interpretation; and where the source itself records academic debate, i used debated. The historical setting of the book (post-exile, reign of Darius, reconstruction of the temple) of the possible date of composition of later parts was also distinguished. One should not read as exhaustive historical reconstruction, but as a context dossier useful for Protestant evangelical study of the book of Zechariah.
